articles.title: The Prophet Who Was Just Like Us
articles.dek: James could have praised Elijah as a spiritual giant. Instead, he went out of his way to tell us that the man whose prayers held back the rain had the same fragile heart we do.
articles.quote: The man whose prayer opened the sky is the same man who once asked God to let him die, and God answered him both times with kindness.
articles.illustration: Spurgeon after the Surrey Gardens disaster
articles.body:
On the evening of October 19, 1856, a twenty-two-year-old preacher named Charles Haddon Spurgeon stood before the largest crowd of his young life. His London congregation had outgrown every building it could rent, so his deacons had booked the Music Hall at the Royal Surrey Gardens, a pleasure park better known for concerts than for sermons. Around ten thousand people filled the hall, and thousands more pressed against the gates outside. Spurgeon had been married only since January, and his wife Susannah had given birth to twin boys just weeks before.

The service had barely begun when someone in the crowd shouted, "Fire!" There was no fire, but the cry raced through the galleries faster than anyone could correct it. People stampeded toward the stairways, and in the crush seven people died and many more were injured. Spurgeon tried to calm the crowd from the pulpit, and at last he had to be helped out of the building, nearly fainting from shock.

What followed was a darkness he would remember for the rest of his life. For days he could hardly open his Bible without weeping, and some newspapers mocked him cruelly. Friends took him to a quiet house outside the city to rest. One day, walking alone in the garden there, a verse rose in his memory: God "exalted him to the highest place and gave him the name that is above every name" (Philippians 2:9). Spurgeon later said the thought that Jesus was still on the throne, whatever happened to a young preacher, broke the darkness open. Within a few weeks he was back in his pulpit.

He went on to preach to millions and became known as the Prince of Preachers. Yet he never pretended the darkness had come only once. He told his congregation honestly that he suffered seasons of depression so heavy he hoped none of them would ever know such wretchedness. He even wrote a lecture for young pastors about what he called "fainting fits," reminding them that faithful servants of God in Scripture had sunk low too. Spurgeon wanted those young men to understand that a powerful ministry and a fragile heart can live in the same person.

The apostle James would have understood him completely. James, the brother of Jesus and the leader of the church in Jerusalem, wrote his letter to "the twelve tribes scattered among the nations" (James 1:1), Jewish Christians who had been pushed from home and were often poor. In chapter 5 he thunders against rich landowners who had withheld the wages of their workers (James 5:4). Then his voice softens, and he begins to pastor the people who were suffering. He tells them to wait like a farmer who watches the sky for autumn and spring rains (James 5:7). He reminds them of Job's perseverance (James 5:11). And then he turns to prayer: "Is anyone among you in trouble? Let them pray. Is anyone happy? Let them sing songs of praise" (James 5:13).

To show what prayer can do, James reaches for one of the most dramatic scenes in the Old Testament. Israel had suffered years of drought under King Ahab, a judgment Elijah had announced to the king's face (1 Kings 17:1). On Mount Carmel, Elijah had faced 450 prophets of Baal alone, and fire had fallen from heaven onto his soaked altar. But the land was still cracked and thirsty. So Elijah climbed to the top of the mountain, "bent down to the ground and put his face between his knees" (1 Kings 18:42). He sent his servant to look out over the Mediterranean. The servant came back and said, "There is nothing there." Elijah sent him again, and again, and again. "Seven times Elijah said, 'Go back'" (1 Kings 18:43). On the seventh trip the servant returned with a strange report: "A cloud as small as a man's hand is rising from the sea" (1 Kings 18:44). Soon the sky turned black with wind, and the heavy rain came.

"The prayer of a righteous person is powerful and effective. Elijah was a human being, even as we are. He prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three and a half years. Again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain, and the earth produced its crops." (James 5:16–18)

The surprising phrase in that passage is the small one in the middle. James could have introduced Elijah as the great prophet, the man of fire. Instead he writes that Elijah was homoiopathēs, a Greek word meaning "of the same nature" or, quite literally, "feeling the same things." The only other place it appears in the New Testament is Acts 14:15, when the crowds at Lystra try to worship Paul and Barnabas as gods, and the two men rush into the crowd crying, "We too are only human, like you." James uses that same word to pull Elijah down from the pedestal and set him beside us.

Every Jewish reader of James knew what happened right after the rain. Queen Jezebel threatened Elijah's life, and the prophet who had stood alone against hundreds ran for his life into the wilderness. He sat under a broom bush and prayed a very different prayer: "I have had enough, LORD. Take my life; I am no better than my ancestors" (1 Kings 19:4). The man whose prayer opened the sky is the same man who once asked God to let him die, and God answered him both times with kindness. He sent the rain, and he also refused the request for death. An angel woke Elijah, gave him warm bread and a jar of water, and let him sleep again before he faced the long road ahead (1 Kings 19:5–8).

One way to read James, then, is that he chose Elijah precisely because of the broom bush. The power of prayer rests on the God who hears, and the "righteous person" James describes is someone who has been put right with God and keeps turning toward him, whatever state their heart is in that day. Even the word "earnestly" in verse 17 is, in Greek, a Hebrew-style expression that reads literally "he prayed with prayer." It describes a person who keeps coming back, face between his knees, sending the servant out a seventh time when the first six reports said nothing.

James also refuses to let anyone carry this alone. Just before Elijah, he writes, "Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed" (James 5:16). Elijah had a servant who climbed the ridge for him. Spurgeon had friends who drove him out of the city and gave him a garden to walk in. Prayer in James's letter is something the church does together, with the elders at the bedside of the sick and friends at the side of the weary (James 5:14).

Many of us were raised to answer every question with "Okay lang ako," even when we are far from okay. We pray for others readily and hide our own heaviness, as if admitting it would shame us or burden the people we love. James gently invites a better way. If you are carrying something today, bring it to God plainly and keep bringing it, the way Elijah sent his servant back to the ridge again and again. Then choose one trusted person, a friend, a spouse, or an elder in your church, and ask them to pray with you this week.

The answer may arrive the way it did on Carmel, as a cloud no bigger than a man's hand. Watch for it, and give thanks for it, because the God who heard a tired prophet on a mountain and fed him under a bush is listening to you with the same patience and the same love.

articles.title: The Staff That Splintered
articles.dek: In the middle of Jerusalem's darkest winter, Ezekiel compared Egypt to a walking stick made of reeds. The image asks what we lean on, and what kind of support we are for the people who lean on us.
articles.quote: The people we lean on were never meant to carry the full weight of our lives, and when we let God carry that weight, we become strong enough to be leaned on ourselves.
articles.illustration: Emily Roebling and the Brooklyn Bridge
articles.body:
In 1872, the man building the Brooklyn Bridge could no longer walk to it. Washington Roebling had taken over the project after his father, the bridge's designer John Roebling, died of tetanus from an injury suffered while surveying the site. Then Washington himself went down into the pressurized caissons beneath the East River and came up with caisson disease, the crippling illness divers now call the bends. He spent the next decade in a room in Brooklyn Heights, watching the towers rise through a window, often too weak to speak to anyone for long. The work did not stop, because his wife Emily refused to let it stop. She taught herself the mathematics of stress and catenary curves, learned the chemistry of steel cable, and carried her husband's instructions to the engineers on site, coming back with their questions. For roughly eleven years, the greatest engineering project in America leaned on a woman who had never been trained as an engineer.

When the bridge opened on May 24, 1883, Emily Roebling was given the honor of being the first to cross it, riding in a carriage and holding a rooster as a sign of victory. A plaque on the bridge today honors all three Roeblings, and it carries a line that has outlived the bridge's builders: "Back of every great work we can find the self-sacrificing devotion of a woman." A suspension bridge is a structure whose entire purpose is to be leaned on, by horses and carts in 1883 and by thousands of cars every day now. It has held because the people behind it were willing to hold.

Ezekiel 29 is about a support that did the opposite. The chapter opens with a precise date: "In the tenth year, in the tenth month on the twelfth day" (Ezekiel 29:1), which scholars place in early January of 587 BC. Ezekiel was living among the exiles in Babylon, but his heart was in Jerusalem, which at that moment was surrounded by Nebuchadnezzar's army. Inside the walls, King Zedekiah had staked everything on a single hope: Egypt. Pharaoh Hophra had promised help, and for a brief, thrilling season it looked like the promise was real. Jeremiah records that when the Egyptian army marched out, the Babylonians actually lifted the siege and withdrew (Jeremiah 37:5). You can imagine the relief in the streets. People must have climbed the walls to watch the enemy leave. Then the Egyptians turned back home, the Babylonians returned, and within months Jerusalem fell.

Into that situation, God gave Ezekiel one of the most vivid pictures in the prophets. First he described Pharaoh as a great crocodile sprawled in the Nile, boasting, "The Nile belongs to me; I made it for myself" (Ezekiel 29:3). Then he turned to what Egypt had been for God's people:

"You have been a staff of reed for the people of Israel. When they grasped you with their hands, you splintered and you tore open their shoulders; when they leaned on you, you broke and their backs were wrenched." (Ezekiel 29:6–7)

Anyone who has walked along a riverbank knows the reeds Ezekiel meant. They grow tall and straight along the Nile, and from a distance they look exactly like a good walking stick. The trouble only shows up when you put your weight on one. A dry reed does not bend gently. It cracks along its length and leaves jagged edges, so the person who trusted it gets hurt twice: once by the fall, and once by the splinters in the hand that held on. The Hebrew phrase is mish'enet qaneh, "a leaning-staff of reed." The word mish'enet comes from the verb sha'an, "to lean, to rest your weight on." It is the same verb in the proverb many of us memorized as children: "Trust in the LORD with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding" (Proverbs 3:5).

Israel had been warned about this exact reed before. More than a century earlier, when Assyria besieged Jerusalem in Hezekiah's day, the Assyrian field commander mocked the city with nearly the same words: "Look, I know you are depending on Egypt, that splintered reed of a staff, which pierces the hand of anyone who leans on it!" (Isaiah 36:6). Even Israel's enemies could see it. Yet the habit of leaning on Egypt kept returning, because Egypt was close, powerful, and visible, and the help it offered looked like the kind of help you could touch.

What makes Ezekiel's word so tender, in one way of reading it, is where God places the blame. He judges Pharaoh for his pride, the arrogance of a man who claimed he had made the Nile. But in verse 16 God also says something to his own people: "Egypt will no longer be a source of confidence for the people of Israel but will be a reminder of their sin in turning to her for help" (Ezekiel 29:16). The Hebrew word for confidence there, mivtach, means the thing you put your trust in. God was gently naming a pattern in Israel's heart. The reed broke because it was a reed. The deeper wound came from asking a reed to do the work of a rock.

Most of us have leaned on a reed at some point. Sometimes it was a person: a boss who promised a promotion, a friend who said they would always be there, a relative abroad whose remittance the whole family's plans depended on. Sometimes it was a thing: a business, a savings account, a reputation, a relationship we hoped would finally make us feel secure. Many of those supports were good gifts. The pain came when we asked them to carry a weight only God can carry, and they splintered under it, as anything human eventually will. Ezekiel's picture gives us permission to stop being angry at reeds for being reeds, and to move our full weight somewhere sturdier.

The passage has a second side, and the Roeblings show it beautifully. The same Bible that warns us not to lean on reeds also shows God's people leaning on each other in healthy ways. When Moses grew too tired to keep his arms raised during the battle with Amalek, "Aaron and Hur held his hands up," "so that his hands remained steady till sunset" (Exodus 17:12). Washington Roebling leaned on Emily, and she held. That kind of support is possible when the one being leaned on is resting on something deeper than herself. A person who has put their full weight on God can be a steady staff for a spouse, a child, a coworker, or an aging parent, because they are not the foundation. They are only passing along strength that comes from beneath them. The people we lean on were never meant to carry the full weight of our lives, and when we let God carry that weight, we become strong enough to be leaned on ourselves.

The chapter just before this one ends with a promise that shows where all of this is heading. After the reeds have broken and the proud nations have fallen silent, God says his people "will live there in safety and will build houses and plant vineyards" (Ezekiel 28:26). People who are always bracing for the next splinter rarely build anything. People who have found a staff that holds can finally plant vines and wait for the harvest.

Today, take a quiet minute and ask God to show you one place where you have been asking a reed to hold you up. Thank him for that person or thing as a gift, and then hand him the weight it was never designed to carry. After that, think of one person who has been leaning on you lately, and be a good staff for them this week with a call, a meal, or an hour of listening. Emily Roebling crossed that bridge first because she had helped hold it up. God is building something in you that is meant to hold others, and it will hold, because he is holding you.

articles.title: The Sheep That Remembered
articles.dek: The longest chapter in the Bible ends with a man admitting he is lost. His last words are also a sign that he is close to being found.
articles.quote: The memory of God's word that makes you ache over how far you have wandered is the same memory that gives you the words to call him back.
articles.body:
In 2001, neuroscientist Keith Kendrick and his colleagues at the Babraham Institute near Cambridge, England, published a short paper in the journal Nature with a title that made readers smile: sheep, they reported, do not forget a face. The animals in their study learned to tell apart the faces of fifty different sheep and could still recognize them about two years later. In related work, the researchers found that when an anxious sheep, separated from its flock, was shown a photograph of a familiar companion, its signs of distress eased. Most of us picture sheep as dim and easily muddled, yet behind those sleepy eyes each animal carries a faithful gallery of the faces it has known and loved.

The surprises kept coming. In 2017, Jenny Morton and her team at the University of Cambridge trained a small flock to recognize photographs of four famous people, among them Barack Obama and the actress Emma Watson. The sheep could pick out those faces even when the photographs showed them from an angle the animals had never seen before. Anyone who grew up in the province and watched a carabao plod home on its own at dusk already suspects that animals remember far more than we credit them with. The research simply confirms it in the case of sheep, the creature the Bible uses most often to describe us. A sheep wanders easily and remembers deeply, and both things are true of it at the same time.

That double truth sits at the very end of one of the most remarkable poems ever written. Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible, 176 verses of devotion to the word of God. It is built as an acrostic, a poem arranged by the alphabet. There are twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and every one of the eight lines in a stanza begins with that stanza's letter. For an ancient reader, moving from the first letter, aleph, to the last, taw, carried a sense of completeness, much the way we speak of covering something "from A to Z." The poet wanted to say everything a human heart could say about loving God's instruction.

And what a love it is. Along the way he has written, "Oh, how I love your law! I meditate on it all day long" (Psalm 119:97), and "Your word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path" (Psalm 119:105). He has told us he rises before dawn to pray (Psalm 119:147) and that God's words taste sweeter than honey (Psalm 119:103). By the time we arrive at the final stanza, the stanza of taw, we expect a triumphant finish from a man who has spent his life close to God.

The last stanza begins, fittingly, with prayer. "May my cry come before you, LORD; give me understanding according to your word" (Psalm 119:169). He asks for rescue, for a song on his lips, for God's hand to be ready to help him (Psalm 119:170–173). He writes, "I long for your salvation, LORD, and your law gives me delight" (Psalm 119:174), and then, "Let me live that I may praise you, and may your laws sustain me" (Psalm 119:175). Then, with one verse left in the whole enormous poem, he says something that has startled readers for nearly three thousand years.

"I have strayed like a lost sheep. Seek your servant, for I have not forgotten your commands." (Psalm 119:176)

The man who loved God's word more than honey ends his masterpiece by confessing that he has wandered off. The Hebrew verb for "strayed" is ta'ah, a word used for an animal that drifts from the flock and for a person who staggers without direction. The word for "lost" is 'obed, which carries the sense of something perishing, something that will come to harm if no one comes for it. Shepherds in the hills of Judea knew that a strayed sheep seldom finds its own way back. It needs to be found.

Yet there is a quiet detail in the Hebrew word order that English cannot fully show. The verse, and therefore the entire psalm, ends on the words lo shakhachti, "I have not forgotten." The very last breath of the longest prayer in Scripture is a statement of memory. One way to read this is that the psalmist's remembering is what made him aware of his straying in the first place. He knew he was lost because he still remembered what home looked like. The commands he had loved were still in him, like the faces stored in the mind of a sheep separated from its flock, and that memory turned into a cry: "Seek your servant."

The memory of God's word that makes you ache over how far you have wandered is the same memory that gives you the words to call him back. The psalmist does not try to walk himself home. He asks the Shepherd to come looking, and he trusts that the Shepherd will.

The rest of Scripture answers that trust with tenderness. Isaiah admits for all of us, "We all, like sheep, have gone astray, each of us has turned to our own way" (Isaiah 53:6). Through Ezekiel, God promises, "I will search for the lost and bring back the strays" (Ezekiel 34:16). Jesus tells the story of a shepherd with a hundred sheep who loses one and asks, "Doesn't he leave the ninety-nine in the open country and go after the lost sheep until he finds it?" (Luke 15:4). He describes his whole mission in the same words the psalmist prayed: "For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost" (Luke 19:10). And he tells us what happens when the Shepherd arrives: "My sheep listen to my voice; I know them, and they follow me" (John 10:27). The lost sheep recognizes him because it remembers him.

Perhaps you are reading this from a place farther from God than you once were. Maybe the prayers you used to say every night have thinned out, or the Bible on your shelf has gathered dust, or a hurt or a habit has led you somewhere you never planned to go. It is easy to believe that a person who drifted should keep quiet until they have fixed themselves. Psalm 119 suggests something gentler. The verse your lola taught you, the chorus from a youth camp years ago, the line of Scripture that still surfaces when you cannot sleep, all of these are signs that you have not forgotten, and that memory is a thread the Shepherd can follow.

The psalmist also shows us that even the most devoted people stray. He had prayed seven times a day and meditated on God's law through the night watches, and still he wandered. If you have been faithful for years and lately feel lost, you are in good company, and the right response is the one he gave, an honest admission joined to a simple request. You do not need polished words. You need only to tell God where you are and ask him to come.

Today, consider writing Psalm 119:176 on a small card or saving it on your phone, and pray it as your own words whenever you notice yourself drifting: "I have strayed like a lost sheep. Seek your servant, for I have not forgotten your commands." Say it on the jeepney, at your desk, or in the quiet before sleep. Then trust that the Shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine is already walking toward you, and that when he calls your name, you will know his voice.

articles.title: The Lamp No One Can Snuff Out
articles.dek: For years an honest analyst watched a cheater grow richer and more admired. Proverbs has a word for the heat that rises in us when the wrong people win, and the gospel has an answer for it.
articles.quote: In Christ, your future hope is the one lamp no one can snuff out.
articles.body:
In 1999, a quiet numbers man named Harry Markopolos was given an assignment that sounded ordinary. His firm in Boston, Rampart Investment Management, kept losing clients to a New York money manager whose fund seemed to make money nearly every month, in good markets and bad. The manager was Bernard Madoff, a former chairman of the Nasdaq stock market, admired, well connected, and generous to charity. Markopolos's bosses wanted him to study Madoff's strategy and build a product that could match it.

He tried. He gathered the return figures, studied the method Madoff claimed to use, and ran the numbers. He later said it took him about five minutes to suspect the results were impossible and a few hours of math to be sure, because no honest strategy could produce a line that smooth. Over the next several years he warned the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission again and again, including in a 2005 memo bluntly titled "The World's Largest Hedge Fund Is a Fraud." Almost no one acted, and the money kept pouring in to Madoff while Markopolos watched a man he knew was cheating grow richer and more celebrated every year.

In December 2008, Madoff confessed. The largest Ponzi scheme in history collapsed almost overnight, and he was later sentenced to 150 years in prison. Markopolos testified before Congress in 2009 and called his book simply No One Would Listen. What stays with me is the long stretch before the collapse, those years when an honest man did careful work while a dishonest one seemed to win. Most of us live in that stretch for a long time before we ever see an ending.

Proverbs speaks straight into that stretch. Our passage closes a section that scholars call "the sayings of the wise" (Proverbs 22:17 to 24:22), a collection of short teachings passed from a father to a son who is preparing for adult life and perhaps for service at the royal court in Jerusalem. The opening part of this section closely resembles an older Egyptian teaching, the Instruction of Amenemope, which was written to train young officials, and that suggests these were lessons for people learning to handle power, money, and ambition. The final saying in the collection takes up a danger every ambitious young person eventually meets, the sight of crooked people getting ahead.

"Do not fret because of evildoers or be envious of the wicked, for the evildoer has no future hope, and the lamp of the wicked will be snuffed out. Fear the LORD and the king, my son, and do not join with rebellious officials, for those two will send sudden destruction on them, and who knows what calamities they can bring?" (Proverbs 24:19–22)

The word translated "fret" is the Hebrew charah, which literally means to burn or to grow hot. Elsewhere in the Old Testament it describes anger flaring up. The father is naming something we feel in our bodies, the heat that rises in the chest when a cheater gets the promotion, the contract, or the applause. The same warning opens Psalm 37: "Do not fret because of those who are evil or be envious of those who do wrong" (Psalm 37:1), and the psalm adds that "like the grass they will soon wither" (Psalm 37:2). Envy and that inner burning travel together, since one wants what the wicked have and the other seethes because they have it.

Then the father gives his reason, and he builds it on two images. The first is "future hope," which translates the Hebrew acharit, meaning the latter end, the way a thing finally turns out. The same word appeared a few verses earlier as a promise to the son himself: "There is surely a future hope for you, and your hope will not be cut off" (Proverbs 23:18; see also 24:14). The father is asking his son to judge a life by its last chapter, the way a careful auditor reads the full books before praising one bright quarter.

The second image is the lamp. In an ancient Israelite home, a small clay oil lamp was often kept burning through the night, and a house with a lit lamp was a house where life carried on. That is why God could promise that David would "always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem" (1 Kings 11:36), meaning his family line would continue. To say that "the lamp of the wicked will be snuffed out" is to say that whatever the wicked have built will one day go dark, with no one left to tend it. Madoff's empire looked like a blazing light for decades, and in one December week it went black.

Verses 21 and 22 can sound strange to modern ears. "Fear the LORD and the king" calls the son to honor God first and to respect the rightful order God allows, and the warning against joining "rebellious officials" uses a Hebrew phrase that suggests people who are always changing sides and angling for advantage. The father knows that envy rarely stays inside the heart. It usually begins as a feeling and ends as an invitation to join the schemers, cut the same corner, and sign the same paper, and the fear of the Lord is what gives a young person the strength to say no.

One way to read the whole saying, then, is as medicine for the heart before envy hardens into a decision. The father's counsel is aimed at his son's own inner life, asking him to cool the heat and keep his eyes on the long road with God. Asaph, the writer of Psalm 73, knew this struggle well. "For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked," he confessed (Psalm 73:3), and he nearly lost his footing until, as he put it, "I entered the sanctuary of God; then I understood their final destiny" (Psalm 73:17). His circumstances stayed the same, but his sight changed when he came near to God.

The gospel carries this truth further than any proverb could. If we are honest, each of us has wanted what was not ours and has cut corners of our own, so the snuffed-out lamp of verse 20 is a sober word for us too. Yet Jesus took that darkness on himself. When he hung on the cross, "darkness came over the whole land until three in the afternoon" (Luke 23:44), and the Light of the world was laid in a tomb. On the third day that light came back, and it can never be put out again. Jesus promised, "Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness, but will have the light of life" (John 8:12), and Peter wrote that God "has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead" (1 Peter 1:3).

That changes how we look at the people who seem to be winning by crooked means. Perhaps it is an officemate who pads expense reports and still gets praised, a contractor who pays under the table and keeps landing projects, or an old classmate whose online lifestyle looks effortless and whose sources of income no one quite understands. The heat will rise, and Scripture does not shame you for feeling it. When it comes, you can name it plainly before God, pray Asaph's way back into the sanctuary, and then ask a harder question about whether anyone is inviting you to cut the same corner this week.

Harry Markopolos lost years of sleep and some standing in his industry, and he kept his integrity. Few of us will ever expose a famous fraud, yet every one of us gets daily chances to stay honest in small rooms where no one is watching. Those choices are oil in the lamp. They may not be applauded, and the cheaters may keep shining for a while, but you are not on their timetable.

So the next time you feel that familiar burning, let it remind you whose light you carry. The schemes of the wicked have a short wick, and your story has a better last chapter. In Christ, your future hope is the one lamp no one can snuff out, and today you can tend it with one quiet, faithful, honest choice.
